name: Chapter 8: Cell: The Unit of Life
description: Cell theory, prokaryotic cells, and every eukaryotic organelle with its NCERT diagram

cards.term: Which Indian scientist discovered the triple helical structure of collagen (1954)?
cards.definition: G.N. Ramachandran

cards.term: What is the Ramachandran plot used for?
cards.definition: Analysing the allowed conformations of proteins

cards.term: Why is the cell the fundamental unit of life?
cards.definition: Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently

cards.term: Who first saw and described a live cell?
cards.definition: Antonie von Leeuwenhoek

cards.term: Who discovered the nucleus?
cards.definition: Robert Brown (1831)

cards.term:
Which is NOT correct:
(a) Robert Brown discovered the cell
(b) Schleiden and Schwann formulated the cell theory
(c) Virchow: cells from pre-existing cells.
cards.definition: (a): Robert Brown discovered the nucleus, not the cell (Robert Hooke named cells)

cards.term: What did Matthias Schleiden (1838) observe?
cards.definition: All plants are composed of different kinds of cells forming tissues

cards.term: What did Theodore Schwann (1839) conclude?
cards.definition: Animal cells have a thin outer layer (plasma membrane) the cell wall is unique to plant cells bodies of animals and plants are cells and products of cells

cards.term: What did Rudolf Virchow (1855) add to the cell theory?
cards.definition: Cells divide and new cells come from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e cellula

cards.term: State the modern cell theory.
cards.definition: (i) All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells. (ii) All cells arise from pre-existing cells.

cards.term: Why was Schleiden and Schwann's cell theory incomplete?
cards.definition: It did not explain how new cells form

cards.term: Eukaryotic vs prokaryotic cell?
cards.definition: Eukaryotic: membrane-bound nucleus. Prokaryotic: no membrane-bound nucleus.

cards.term: What is the cytoplasm?
cards.definition: The semi-fluid matrix filling the cell: the main arena of cellular activities

cards.term: Which organelle is found in all cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic?
cards.definition: Ribosomes (non-membrane bound)

cards.term: Besides the cytoplasm, where are ribosomes found in a cell?
cards.definition: Inside chloroplasts and mitochondria, and on rough ER

cards.term: Which non-membrane bound organelle in animal cells helps in cell division?
cards.definition: Centrosome

cards.term: Smallest cells, and their size (NCERT)?
cards.definition: Mycoplasmas: NCERT prints "0.3 mm"

cards.term: Is Mycoplasma really 0.3 mm long? (correction)
cards.definition: No: about 0.3 µm (0.1–0.3 µm). "mm" in NCERT is a misprint; 0.3 mm would be visible to the naked eye.

cards.term: Size of typical bacteria and of human RBCs?
cards.definition: Bacteria: 3–5 µm (Fig 8.2 says 1–2 µm). Human RBC: about 7.0 µm in diameter.

cards.term: Largest isolated single cell?
cards.definition: The egg of an ostrich

cards.term: Which are some of the longest cells?
cards.definition: Nerve cells

cards.term: Name the cell shapes shown in Figure 8.1.
cards.definition:
RBC: round, biconcave.
WBC: amoeboid.
Columnar epithelial: long, narrow.
Nerve cell: branched, long.
Tracheid: elongated.
Mesophyll: round, oval.

cards.term: Rank by size (Figure 8.2): PPLO, virus, bacterium, eukaryotic cell.
cards.definition: Virus 0.02–0.2 µm < PPLO ~0.1 µm < bacterium 1–2 µm < eukaryotic cell 10–20 µm

cards.term: Name the prokaryotes listed by NCERT.
cards.definition: Bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms)

cards.term: Which prokaryote lacks a cell wall?
cards.definition: Mycoplasma

cards.term: What are plasmids?
cards.definition: Small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA in many bacteria

cards.term: What do plasmids give bacteria, and how are they used?
cards.definition: Unique phenotypic characters, e.g. antibiotic resistance; used to monitor bacterial transformation with foreign DNA

cards.term: Which is the only eukaryote-like organelle in prokaryotes?
cards.definition: Ribosomes

cards.term: What is a mesosome?
cards.definition: Infoldings of the cell membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae): characteristic of prokaryotes

cards.term: Functions of the mesosome?
cards.definition: Cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration, secretion, more membrane surface area and enzymes

cards.term: What are chromatophores? Where?
cards.definition: Pigment-containing membranous extensions into the cytoplasm, in cyanobacteria

cards.term: Three layers of the bacterial cell envelope, outside in?
cards.definition: Glycocalyx → cell wall → plasma membrane

cards.term: On what is the Gram positive / Gram negative division based?
cards.definition: Differences in the cell envelope and whether it takes up the Gram stain

cards.term: Slime layer vs capsule?
cards.definition: Both are glycocalyx: slime layer is a loose sheath; capsule is thick and tough

cards.term: What does the bacterial cell wall do?
cards.definition: Determines shape and stops the cell bursting or collapsing

cards.term: Three parts of a bacterial flagellum?
cards.definition: Filament, hook, basal body (filament is the longest)

cards.term: Pili vs fimbriae? Do they help movement?
cards.definition: Neither helps motility. Pili: elongated tubular protein structures. Fimbriae: small bristle-like fibres that help attach to rocks and host tissues.

cards.term: Prokaryotic ribosomes: size, subunits and location?
cards.definition: 70S (50S + 30S), about 15 × 20 nm, associated with the plasma membrane

cards.term: What is a polysome?
cards.definition: Several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA, translating it into proteins

cards.term: What are inclusion bodies? Examples?
cards.definition: Reserve material free in the cytoplasm, not membrane-bound: phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules

cards.term: Where are gas vacuoles found?
cards.definition: In blue green, and purple and green photosynthetic bacteria

cards.term: Which organisms are eukaryotes?
cards.definition: All protists, plants, animals and fungi

cards.term: What do plant cells have that animal cells lack?
cards.definition: Cell wall, plastids, a large central vacuole

cards.term: What do animal cells have that almost all plant cells lack?
cards.definition: Centrioles

cards.term: Figure 8.3 (a) · Plant cell
Figure 8.3 (b) · Animal cell
Which cells were used in the chemical studies of the cell membrane?
cards.definition: Human red blood cells

cards.term: What are cell membranes mainly made of?
cards.definition: Lipids (mainly phospholipids in a bilayer) and proteins; also cholesterol and carbohydrate

cards.term: How are phospholipids arranged in the membrane?
cards.definition: Polar heads outwards, hydrophobic tails inwards, away from water

cards.term: Protein and lipid in the human RBC membrane?
cards.definition: About 52% protein and 40% lipid

cards.term: Integral vs peripheral proteins?
cards.definition: Peripheral: on the surface. Integral: partially or totally buried in the membrane.

cards.term: Who proposed the fluid mosaic model, and when?
cards.definition: Singer and Nicolson, 1972

cards.term: What does "fluid" in the fluid mosaic model mean?
cards.definition: The quasi-fluid lipid lets proteins move laterally within the bilayer (measured as fluidity)

cards.term: Which functions depend on membrane fluidity?
cards.definition: Cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, cell division

cards.term: Figure 8.4 · Fluid mosaic model
What is passive transport?
cards.definition: Movement across the membrane without energy, e.g. simple diffusion along the concentration gradient

cards.term: What is osmosis?
cards.definition: Movement of water by diffusion

cards.term: How do polar molecules cross the membrane?
cards.definition: Via a carrier protein (they cannot pass through the nonpolar bilayer)

cards.term: What is active transport? Example?
cards.definition: Movement against the concentration gradient using ATP, e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump

cards.term: Functions of the cell wall?
cards.definition: Shape, protection from mechanical damage and infection, cell-to-cell interaction, barrier to undesirable macromolecules

cards.term: Cell wall of algae vs other plants?
cards.definition: Algae: cellulose, galactans, mannans, minerals like CaCO₃. Other plants: cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins.

cards.term: Primary vs secondary wall?
cards.definition: Primary: of a young cell, capable of growth. Secondary: formed on the inner side (towards the membrane) as the cell matures.

cards.term: What is the middle lamella made of, and what does it do?
cards.definition: Mainly calcium pectate; glues neighbouring cells together

cards.term: What are plasmodesmata?
cards.definition: Connections through the cell wall and middle lamella linking the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells

cards.term: Which organelles make up the endomembrane system?
cards.definition: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, vacuoles

cards.term: Why are mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes excluded from the endomembrane system?
cards.definition: Their functions are not coordinated with it

cards.term: Into which compartments does the ER divide the cell?
cards.definition: Luminal (inside ER) and extra luminal (cytoplasm)

cards.term: RER vs SER: structure and function?
cards.definition: RER: ribosomes on the surface protein synthesis and secretion continuous with the outer nuclear membrane. SER: no ribosomes lipid synthesis (steroid hormones in animals).

cards.term: Figure 8.5 · Endoplasmic reticulum
Who first observed Golgi bodies, and when?
cards.definition: Camillo Golgi, 1898

cards.term: What are cisternae, and their size?
cards.definition: Flat, disc-shaped sacs of the Golgi, 0.5–1.0 µm across, stacked in parallel

cards.text: The Golgi has a convex {{c1::cis (forming)}} face and a concave {{c2::trans (maturing)}} face; ER vesicles fuse with the {{c3::cis}} face.

cards.term: Main function of the Golgi apparatus?
cards.definition: Packaging materials for delivery inside the cell or secretion; modifies proteins from the ER

cards.term: What does the Golgi form besides packaged proteins?
cards.definition: Glycoproteins and glycolipids

cards.term: How are lysosomes formed?
cards.definition: By packaging in the Golgi apparatus

cards.term: What do lysosomes contain, and at what pH are these active?
cards.definition: Hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases), optimally active at acidic pH

cards.term: What is the tonoplast?
cards.definition: The single membrane around the vacuole

cards.term: How much of a plant cell can the vacuole occupy?
cards.definition: Up to 90%

cards.term: Why is ion concentration higher in the vacuole than in the cytoplasm?
cards.definition: The tonoplast transports ions against concentration gradients into the vacuole

cards.term: Contractile vacuole vs food vacuole?
cards.definition: Contractile (Amoeba): osmoregulation and excretion. Food vacuole (protists): formed by engulfing food.

cards.term: Lysosomes and vacuoles are both endomembrane structures. How do their functions differ?
cards.definition: Lysosomes digest macromolecules with enzymes; vacuoles store water, sap and wastes, and regulate osmosis

cards.term: Shape and size of a typical mitochondrion?
cards.definition: Sausage-shaped or cylindrical; diameter 0.2–1.0 µm (avg 0.5), length 1.0–4.1 µm

cards.term: What are cristae, and why are they there?
cards.definition: Infoldings of the inner membrane towards the matrix; they increase surface area

cards.term: Figure 8.7 · Mitochondrion (L.S.)
Why are mitochondria called the cell's power houses?
cards.definition: They are sites of aerobic respiration and produce ATP

cards.term: What does the mitochondrial matrix contain for protein synthesis?
cards.definition: Single circular DNA, a few RNAs, 70S ribosomes

cards.term: How do mitochondria divide?
cards.definition: By fission

cards.term: Match: cristae, cisternae, thylakoids.
cards.definition: Cristae: infoldings in mitochondria. Cisternae: disc-shaped sacs in Golgi. Thylakoids: flat sacs in chloroplast stroma.

cards.term: Where are plastids found?
cards.definition: All plant cells and euglenoids

cards.term: Name the three types of plastids and their pigments.
cards.definition: Chloroplasts: chlorophyll, carotenoids. Chromoplasts: fat-soluble carotenoids (yellow, orange, red). Leucoplasts: colourless.

cards.text: Leucoplasts: {{c1::amyloplasts}} store starch (e.g. potato), {{c2::elaioplasts}} store oils and fats, and {{c3::aleuroplasts}} store proteins.
cards.extra: Memory aid: Amylo = starch (amylose), Elaio = oil (Greek elaion, olive oil), Aleuro = protein (aleurone layer).

cards.term: Size and number of chloroplasts?
cards.definition: 5–10 µm long, 2–4 µm wide; from 1 per cell (Chlamydomonas) to 20–40 per mesophyll cell

cards.term: Which chloroplast membrane is less permeable?
cards.definition: The inner membrane

cards.term: What are grana and stroma lamellae?
cards.definition: Grana: stacks of thylakoids like piles of coins. Stroma lamellae: flat tubules connecting thylakoids of different grana.

cards.term: Where are chlorophyll pigments located?
cards.definition: In the thylakoids

cards.term: What does the chloroplast stroma contain?
cards.definition: Enzymes for carbohydrate and protein synthesis, small double-stranded circular DNA, ribosomes

cards.term: Which reactions occur in grana and stroma?
cards.definition: Grana: light reactions. Stroma: dark reactions.

cards.term: Why is it thought mitochondria and chloroplasts were once bacteria? (beyond NCERT)
cards.definition: Both have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membranes, and divide by fission: the endosymbiotic theory

cards.term: Who first observed ribosomes, and when?
cards.definition: George Palade, 1953

cards.term: What are ribosomes made of?
cards.definition: RNA and proteins, with no membrane

cards.term: Subunits of 80S and 70S ribosomes?
cards.definition: 80S: 60S + 40S. 70S: 50S + 30S.

cards.term: What does 'S' mean in 70S and 80S?
cards.definition: Svedberg unit: sedimentation coefficient, indirectly a measure of density and size

cards.term: Why is 60S + 40S = 80S and not 100S?
cards.definition: Svedberg units measure how fast particles sediment, which depends on shape and size, so they do not add up

cards.term: What makes up the cytoskeleton?
cards.definition: Microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments

cards.term: Functions of the cytoskeleton?
cards.definition: Mechanical support, motility, maintaining cell shape

cards.term: Cilia vs flagella?
cards.definition: Cilia: small, work like oars to move the cell or fluid. Flagella: longer, move the cell.

cards.term: What is the axoneme?
cards.definition: The core of a cilium or flagellum: microtubules parallel to its long axis

cards.term: What is the 9+2 array?
cards.definition: Nine peripheral microtubule doublets + a pair of central microtubules

cards.term: Figure 8.10 (b) · Section of a cilium / flagellum
How many radial spokes in a cilium?
cards.definition: Nine

cards.term: From what do cilia and flagella emerge?
cards.definition: Centriole-like basal bodies

cards.term: Is the bacterial flagellum like the eukaryotic one?
cards.definition: No; structurally different (no 9+2 axoneme)

cards.term: What does a centrosome contain?
cards.definition: Usually two centrioles, perpendicular to each other, in amorphous pericentriolar material

cards.term: Structure of a centriole?
cards.definition: Cartwheel of nine peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin; central hub joined to them by radial spokes

cards.term: Doublets or triplets: cilium vs centriole?
cards.definition: Cilium axoneme: 9 doublets + 2 central (9+2). Centriole: 9 triplets, no central pair (9+0).

cards.term: What do centrioles form?
cards.definition: The basal body of cilia or flagella, and spindle fibres in animal cell division

cards.term: Who named chromatin?
cards.definition: Flemming (material stained by basic dyes)

cards.term: What is the perinuclear space?
cards.definition: The 10–50 nm space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope

cards.term: What is the outer nuclear membrane continuous with?
cards.definition: The endoplasmic reticulum (it bears ribosomes)

cards.term: What passes through nuclear pores?
cards.definition: RNA and protein molecules, in both directions

cards.term: Figure 8.11 · Structure of nucleus
Name two kinds of cells without a nucleus.
cards.definition: Erythrocytes of many mammals and sieve tube cells

cards.term: What happens in the nucleolus?
cards.definition: Active ribosomal RNA synthesis; it is not membrane-bound

cards.term: Which cells have larger, more numerous nucleoli?
cards.definition: Cells actively carrying out protein synthesis

cards.term: What does chromatin contain?
cards.definition: DNA, basic proteins (histones), non-histone proteins, RNA

cards.term: Length of DNA in a single human cell, and in how many chromosomes?
cards.definition: About 2 metres, in 46 (23 pairs)

cards.term: What are kinetochores?
cards.definition: Disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere (primary constriction)

cards.text:
Centromere position: {{c1::metacentric}} = middle (equal arms)
{{c2::sub-metacentric}} = slightly off-centre
{{c3::acrocentric}} = close to one end
{{c4::telocentric}} = terminal.

cards.term: Identify the four chromosome types in Figure 8.13 (left to right).
cards.definition: Metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric

cards.term: What is a satellite chromosome?
cards.definition: A chromosome with a non-staining secondary constriction that makes a small fragment appear

cards.term: What are microbodies?
cards.definition: Minute membrane-bound vesicles with enzymes, in both plant and animal cells

cards.term: Organelle membranes
cards.definition: Mitochondria, chloroplasts, nucleus: Double; ER, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole: Single; Ribosome, centrosome: None
